big: Two funds, one gave 28% and the other gave 14% in the same year. Which is the better fund? The question hides a trap: they may not be playing the same game.

lines: This mid cap fund gave 28% and your large cap gave 14%. Why would I hold the large cap?
Good question. First see how SEBI sorts funds into categories, then watch both funds over a longer stretch.

alt: Three lines for a liquid fund, a large cap fund and a mid cap fund over ten made-up years
caps: Three made-up funds start with ₹100 each: a liquid fund, a large cap fund and a mid cap fund.
In year 1 the mid cap gains 28% and the large cap 14%. This is the number Rohan saw.
Then the mid cap falls harder: about 25% in year 3, against 9% for the large cap.
After ten years the mid cap ended below the large cap here, after a much rougher ride.
Different jobs, different risk. Compare a fund with others in its own category.

small: Overnight: Low. Small cap: Very High
alt: Six bars rising from low to very high risk
caps: The riskometer is a gauge on every scheme. It has six levels, from Low to Very High.
It is based on what the fund actually holds, and it is updated regularly.
An overnight fund sits near the left. A small cap fund sits at the right end.
It shows how risky the holdings are. It does not show how much the fund will earn.

title: What a category label tells you
stops: Who it should be compared with
h: What a category label tells you
alt: A shield with what a SEBI category label does and does not tell you
caps: SEBI sorts schemes into categories so that funds with the same label follow the same rules.
A large cap fund must keep a minimum in large caps, so it cannot drift into small caps.
But the label tells you the rules, not the results. Two funds in a category can earn very differently.

q: Rohan says his mid cap fund gave 28% last year and Meena's large cap gave 14%, so the large cap should go. What is the fair reply?
opts: Different jobs: a mid cap can fall far harder, so one year decides little
Agree, since the higher return shows the mid cap is better managed
Agree, but only if the mid cap beats the large cap two years in a row
Disagree, since large cap funds are always the higher earner over time
why: The mid cap fund is built to take more risk. In the film it fell about 25% in a year, and ended below the large cap.
A higher return in one year can come from taking more risk, not from better management. The next year can reverse it.
Two years is still too short to judge. Risk shows in the falls, and a longer stretch includes them.
No category always earns more. Mid caps have done better in some stretches and worse in others.

q: A scheme's riskometer reads Very High. What does it tell Meena?
opts: The fund is expected to earn the highest returns of any scheme
The fund has been ranked best by SEBI among all schemes this year
The fund cannot be sold at all during the first year after buying
The fund's holdings carry a very high level of risk right now
why: The riskometer shows risk, not return. A Very High reading means big swings, in both directions, are possible.
SEBI does not rank funds. The riskometer is a gauge of risk and not a prize for performance or quality.
The riskometer has nothing to do with lock-ins or when you can sell. Those rules sit in the scheme document.
The riskometer reflects what the fund holds and is updated regularly. Very High means large swings are possible.

q: A small cap fund returned 30% this year and a liquid fund 6.5%. Rohan calls the liquid fund poor. What is a fair comparison?
opts: Ignore returns and compare only the fund house's name
Compare the two directly, since the higher return always wins
Compare each fund only with others in its own category
Compare them only by the size of the NAV in rupees
why: A fund house name does not tell you how the fund did against others of its kind.
A higher return from a riskier fund is not a better fund. The small cap took far more risk to earn it.
Funds in one category follow the same rules and carry similar risk, so comparing them is fair.
NAV in rupees is only the unit price. A fund with a high NAV is not better than one with a low NAV.

q: Two large cap funds both follow SEBI's large cap rule. Over five years one gave 15% a year and the other 11%. What does the category label tell Meena?
opts: That the 11% fund must now be moved to another category
That both will give 13% a year, the average of the two figures
That the 15% fund broke the rules by earning so much more
Both follow the large cap rule, though results can still differ
why: A lower return does not change the category. The category depends on what the fund holds.
Labels do not set a return, and the average has no special meaning for either fund.
Earning more does not break any rule. Both funds can follow the category rule and still earn differently.
The label sets rules for what the fund holds. How well the manager does inside those rules can differ.

pts: Compare funds inside their own category, not across categories.
The riskometer shows risk, not return. It is based on what the fund holds.
A label tells you the rules, not the results.
